titre: Four Rules for Accusing a Microbe
accroche: On March 24, 1882, Robert Koch announces he has found the culprit of a disease that kills, by his reckoning, one person in seven worldwide
contenu_vulgarise:
On the evening of March 24, 1882, Robert Koch appears before the Physiological Society of Berlin. He has just demonstrated that a specific microbe, invisible to the naked eye, causes tuberculosis, a disease that kills, by his own statistics, one person in seven worldwide, and up to a third of working-age adults.

## Seeing the Microbe Is Not Enough to Accuse It

Before Koch, several researchers had already observed rods in the tissues of tuberculosis patients, without being able to prove that these rods were the cause of the disease rather than a mere consequence. Koch develops a stain that makes the bacilli sharply visible under the microscope, blue against a background of brown tissue, then isolates them from diseased tissue and, after several months of trials, manages to grow them outside any living organism, on a medium of coagulated serum.

He then takes the decisive step: he inoculates this pure culture, obtained in the laboratory and never in contact with a sick organism, into healthy animals. They develop tuberculosis, and Koch finds in their tissues the same bacillus he had isolated at the outset. The loop is closed: the microbe is present in all cases of the disease, it can be grown outside the body, and its reintroduction into a healthy host reproduces the disease.

## A Method More Than a Discovery

In 1884, Koch formalizes this approach into four criteria, known ever since as Koch's postulates: the microbe must be present in all cases of the disease, absent in healthy subjects, culturable outside the organism, and capable of reproducing the disease once reinoculated into a healthy host. These criteria become the reference method for establishing that a specific microbe causes a specific disease, well beyond tuberculosis, for the whole of nascent bacteriology.

## The Shift

What Koch invented is not merely a diagnosis: it is a protocol of proof, reproducible by any researcher with a microscope and a laboratory, which turns an intuition into a demonstration verifiable by third parties. The postulates will themselves be revised later, since certain infectious agents, such as viruses or certain bacteria that cannot be cultured in the laboratory, do not conform to them, but the principle underlying them, demanding reproducible proof before accusing an organism, remains the backbone of infectious disease medicine. Koch receives the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1905 for the whole of this work.

citation.texte: Statistics teach that one-seventh of all human beings die of tuberculosis, and that, if one considers only the productive middle-age groups, tuberculosis carries away one-third and often more of these.
citation.source: “The Aetiology of Tuberculosis,” read before the Physiological Society of Berlin on March 24, 1882

carte.punch: A microbe that killed one human in seven ended up having to obey four simple rules.
carte.idee: On March 24, 1882, Robert Koch demonstrates that a specific bacillus causes tuberculosis. He formalizes his method in 1884: four criteria a microbe must meet before it can be accused of a disease. These postulates become the reference for all of nascent bacteriology.

quiz.question: What distinguishes Koch's demonstration from a mere observation of the bacillus under the microscope?
choix: He was the first researcher to observe rods in the tissues of tuberculosis patients
He obtained the unanimous agreement of the Physiological Society of Berlin before publishing his results
He used a more powerful microscope than his predecessors
He grew the bacillus outside any organism, then reproduced the disease by reinoculating it into a healthy animal
quiz.explication: Other researchers had already seen rods without proving their causal role. Koch takes a step that observation alone does not allow: isolating the microbe, growing it outside any organism, then reproducing the disease by reinoculating it into a healthy host, the loop his postulates would formalize in 1884. Neither his audience's agreement nor the power of his microscope constitutes causal proof.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What are the four criteria formalized by Koch in 1884 for accusing a microbe of a disease?
choix: Present in all cases, absent in healthy subjects, culturable outside the organism, capable of reproducing the disease
Visible under the microscope, stained blue, heat-resistant, transmissible by air
Present in most patients, absent in all healthy subjects, incurable, fatal in one case in seven
Isolated in the laboratory, patented, published in a peer-reviewed journal, recognized by a Nobel Prize
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The four postulates of 1884 require that the microbe be present in all cases of the disease, absent in healthy subjects, culturable outside the organism, and capable of reproducing the disease once reinoculated into a healthy host.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What limit do Koch's postulates run into, according to the entry?
choix: Certain infectious agents, such as viruses, do not conform to them
They apply only to respiratory diseases like tuberculosis
They require a microscope too powerful to be used outside Germany
They were entirely abandoned upon Koch's death
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Certain infectious agents, such as viruses or certain bacteria that cannot be cultured in the laboratory, do not conform to the four postulates, which have since been revised without their principle of reproducible proof disappearing.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What technique does Koch develop to make the bacilli sharply visible?
choix: A stain that makes them appear blue against a background of brown tissue
An electron microscope able to magnify the image a thousand times
A red dye that marks only the surrounding healthy tissue
A freezing technique that immobilizes moving bacilli
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Koch develops a stain that makes the bacilli sharply visible under the microscope, appearing blue against a background of brown tissue.
